newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius trims 1996 growth forecast to 5.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius trims 1996 growth forecast to 5.7 pct.

text.p: The Indian Ocean island of Mauritius on Tuesday trimmed its economic growth forecast for 1996 to 5.7 percent from an earlier forecast of 5.8 percent in May.

Finance Minister Vaasant Bunwaree told parliament "After an economic growth of 5.3 percent in 1995, the overall growth rate in 1996 will be around 5.7 percent which is slightly lower than the 5.8 percent projected earlier."
He blamed the slightly lower economic growth to a lower sugar production of 590,000 tonnes expected for the 1996 crop season from an earlier forecast of 610,000 tonnes.
For the next 3 years, Bunwaree aimed at achieving growth between 5.5 percent to 6.5 percent.
Inflation is expected to be 6.5 percent for the calendar year 1996 from 6.0 percent in 1995.
"Inflation pressures in the economy have intensified, due mainly to the increase in the value of the dollar and the pound sterling," Bunwaree said.
"We, in government are very much concerned about this problem and fighting inflation will be one of the top priority of our fiscal and monetary policies," he added.
Bunwaree said medium term inflation in Mauritius has been targetted to below 5.0 percent by the end of the century.
Bunwaree forecast the trade deficit at 7.0 billion rupees, unchanged from 1995.
But he told parliament that would be offset by surpluses in services and capital accounts to give an overall surplus of 1.0 billion rupees in the overall balance of payments.
"Thus the level of official foreign exchange reserves is expected to reach around 24 weeks worth of imports by the end of the current financial year (30 June 1997)," Bunwaree said.

"At the end of November 1996, foreign exchange reserves of the Bank of Mauritius (central bank) stood at 15.383 billion rupees, representing import cover of 21.2 weeks, and as today, the cover is equivalent to 21.9 weeks of imports," he added.
Bunwaree also said the 1996/97 budget deficit had been revised to 4.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from an earlier forecast of 3.9 percent made last August.

"At this stage, indications are that, after allowing for the cost of implementing the package negotiated with Trade Unions and for variations in revenue and expenditure, the overall budget deficit would be contained at around 3.650 billion rupees, that is about 4.6 percent of GDP," Bunwaree said.
The budget deficit in 1995/96 was 5.8 percent of GDP.
Bunwaree added he was aiming at reducing the budget deficit to 2.0 percent by the financial year 1999/2000.
